articles.title: Key races yet to be called include nail-biters in Colorado and Mississippi
articles.summary: Democrats on Tuesday comprehensively routed their Republican rivals , regaining control of the U.S. House, U.S. Senate and statehouses across the country. It was one of the most lopsided midterm performances in modern U.S. history. Coming into the night, Republicans held 53 of the Senate's 100 seats; Democrats held 45. To wrest back control of the Senate, Democrats needed a net gain of at least four seats. As at 11:30 a.m. ET on Wednesday, the Democrats had won 54 Senate seats to the GOP's 44 — and they could wind up winning as many as 56 once all the votes are counted in Alaska and Mississippi, where key races have yet to be called. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed defeated Mike Rogers in one of the most closely watched races. James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, becoming the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in the Lone Star State since 1988. Annie Andrews beat GOP Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina to flip a Senate seat. In Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson defeated incumbent GOP Sen. Susan Collins, putting an end to her three-decade tenure. Sen. Jon Ossoff comfortably won reelection in Georgia. Other Senate seats to flip to the Democratic Party included Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Sherrod Brown in Ohio, Josh Turek in Iowa and Adam Hamilton in Kansas. In the 435-seat House, the GOP held 218 seats; the Democrats held 214. To retake control of the House , Democrats needed a net gain of three seats. The AP said early Wednesday that they had exceeded that figure; the latest estimates show that the party is on track to win its largest majority since 2008. There were also 36 gubernatorial races and numerous ballot measures to keep an eye on. Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia became the first Black woman elected governor in U.S. history, while Democrat Amy Acton became the first woman elected governor of Ohio. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds became the state's first Black governor-elect. El-Sayed will be America's first Muslim senator. President Trump, whose approval ratings are at or near all-time lows, distanced himself from mounting Republican losses in a post on Truth Social on Tuesday night. "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" Trump wrote. "Thank you for your attention to this matter." The president later said he was willing to work with Democrats while also suggesting he wouldn’t hesitate to use his veto powers. articles.title: Dow jumps around 1,300 points in response to Democrats' control of Congress
articles.summary: US stocks jumped on Wednesday after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in a seismic midterm election, paving the way for a divided government. The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose 2.8%, or around 1,400 points, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) climbed 1.7%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) traded up by 1.8% as Apple ( AAPL ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ) stocks touched record highs. Markets swiftly repriced a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate — and the potential for ballot measures and newly elected officials to restrict data center construction . Chip stocks, including Nvidia ( NVDA ) and Micron ( MU ), fell more than 1%. Meanwhile, other parts of the tech sector offset some of those losses with Apple ( AAPL ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ) each hitting all-time highs. Investors will also be watching for policy actions on housing and pharmaceuticals in the aftermath of the election. As Yahoo Finance's Jared Blikre pointed out on Tuesday , midterm elections have a history of shaping stock performance in the near term but don't tend to move markets much over the long term. On the economic front, ISM and S&P data showed that US services activity expanded at a slower pace in October as businesses continued to grapple with elevated costs. Private-sector hiring , meanwhile, continued to show strength in October as an ADP report indicated "pretty solid job growth." Earnings continue to roll in. AMD ( AMD ) posted a Q3 earnings beat , while McDonald's ( MCD ) grappled with slowing same-store sales growth . Duolingo ( DUOL ) stock soared over 30% on strong user growth. articles.title: Trump is reportedly asking his advisers if Hegseth should remain in his job
articles.summary: Washington — President Trump has been asking advisers around him and on the phone whether Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should stay in his job, following Republicans' catastrophic losses Tuesday night, multiple sources familiar with the matter tell CBS News. Some White House aides have predicted some of the blame for GOP midterm losses will be trained on Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, who both played big roles in guidance on the Iran war. Still, other sources said the president hasn't decided to replace Hegseth. Before the election, Democrats were already trying to impeach Hegseth, and the likelihood of an impeachment effort could increase with Democrats holding strong majorities in both chambers. Vice President JD Vance is blaming the war for the GOP defeat. "The reason we lost is the war," he said in a lengthy post on X Wednesday morning. One source told CBS News that GOP Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is being floated as a possible replacement for Hegseth, arguing DeSantis could go through Senate confirmation in the lame-duck period and then take the post when his term as governor expires Jan. 5. Asked for comment about reports that Hegseth's future as defense secretary, White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement that Mr. Trump "has full confidence in Secretary Hegseth." In the statement, Kelly also praised the military operations in Iran and Venezuela and Hegseth's efforts to reverse the Biden Pentagon's prioritizing of "DEI and woke ideology." articles.title: Vance blames Iran war for GOP's midterm losses in social media post
articles.summary: Vice President JD Vance blamed Republicans’ sweeping midterm losses on the war with Iran on Wednesday, arguing that voters who backed President Donald Trump in 2024 turned against the Republican Party over the conflict. “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote in a lengthy social media post . The remarks represent a striking acknowledgment from the vice president that the administration’s handling of the Iran conflict has become a political liability for Republicans, even as his boss has defended the approach to the war. Vance also suggested that Republicans who supported the war should concede the political costs rather than look for alternative explanations for the Tuesday results. “To the people who are pissed off and want to say, ‘I told you so’: you’re right, you did tell us so,” he wrote in his lengthy post. “Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview.” Vance’s assessment of the GOP wreckage quickly gained praise from some close to Trump. Donald Trump Jr., the president’s eldest son, reposted Vance’s autopsy, adding: “Every word of this is 💯💯💯.” The vice president argued that Republican turnout was strong Tuesday but that many voters who supported his ticket two years ago instead cast ballots for Democrats. “Our voters did show up,” Vance wrote. “But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.” Vance pointed to four answers an unnamed trusted pollster gave him about what voters said would win their votes back: ending the war, focusing on cost of living, putting “America First” and changing the U.S. relationship to Israel. Vance — who was initially one of the least supportive members of the administration on the war in Iran but ultimately took on a public-facing role in negotiating failed peace deals over the summer — said that people might continue to argue about whether the war was a worthwhile price to pay for “losing the Senate for the next 6 years” but that they should start from acknowledging it was, in fact, the reason. “Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest,” he wrote. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.” The president seemed less willing to back down on Iran in a phone call with POLITICO on Tuesday night. Trump said he was hearing that the midterm losses could be related to oil prices driven higher by the conflict, but that he remained “totally convinced” that using military force in Iran was the “absolutely correct” decision. “And it continues to be,” Trump said. Trump also didn’t rule out continued strikes after the midterms. “We're going to take a look,” Trump said Tuesday night. “I think if we see any opportunity to do one thing or another, we're going to do what's best for this country.” The president did rule out the use of nuclear weapons on the country, speculation that recently made the rounds after being raised by conservative commentator Tucker Carlson, who has sharply criticized the administration’s interventions in Iran and its support of Israel. In his early analysis of the results, Vance also appeared to anticipate and try to preempt an internal Republican fight over how the party should respond to its losses, particularly on the administration’s hardline immigration stance and use of ICE. “Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty,” Vance said. “I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement — by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you.” Vance, who ran for president in 2024 before becoming Trump’s vice president, is a known 2028 presidential contender who Trump openly muses could take up the MAGA mantle. But both Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the other top contender in Trump’s administration, have been publicly tied to the unpopular war in Iran through their continued roles in negotiations and policy decisions. The president’s continued support for the war sets up a headwind for the potential candidates in 2028 — a circumstance Vance acknowledged and sought to get ahead of on Wednesday morning with a call to action for voters to join him in turning policy around. “To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country,” Vance wrote. articles.title: From Georgia to Michigan, midterm voters deliver a series of historic firsts
articles.summary: The results of the 2026 midterm elections have delivered a series of historic wins, with candidates across the country breaking barriers — and glass ceilings — at the ballot box. The results come amid a sweeping Democratic victory in a battle for control of Congress, with both chambers shifting from Republican to Democratic majorities starting in January. Among the headline-making victories are the nation's first Black woman governor, the first Native American woman governor, the first Muslim U.S. senator and the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. Here's a closer look at the historic wins of the 2026 midterms. U.S. Senate Abdul El-Sayed Democrat Abdul El-Sayed makes remarks in Detroit, Mich., on Nov. 4. Anadolu via Getty Images The Democrat became the first Muslim U.S. senator in American history when he won Michigan's hotly contested Senate race against Republican Mike Rogers. The victory came after El-Sayed's Democratic primary rival, Haley Stevens, endorsed Rogers just days before the election. Peggy Flanagan Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, speaks at an election night event in St. Paul on Tuesday. AP Photo/Abbie Parr The Democratic lieutenant governor of Minnesota became the first Native American woman elected to the U.S. Senate. She is Ojibwe and a member of the White Earth Nation. Chris Pappas New Hampshire Democratic Senate candidate Rep. Chris Pappas, right, speaks at an election night event, with Vann Bentley, left, in Manchester. AP Photo/Reba Saldanha The Democratic New Hampshire representative was elected to the U.S. Senate, making him the first openly gay man elected to serve in that congressional chamber. Governor Amy Acton Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton waves during an election night event in Columbus. AP Photo/Carolyn Kaster Acton, the former director of the Ohio Department of Health, became Ohio's first woman governor and the first Jewish governor in the state's history. She defeated her opponent, Republican businessman Vivek Ramaswamy, for the seat after a hostile race in its final weeks leading up to the election. An attack ad from the Ramaswamy campaign featured Acton's estranged mother, who called her daughter a liar. The ad drew widespread criticism of Ramaswamy and an outpouring of support for Acton, who has said she was abused as a child. Marsha Blackburn Tennessee Republican gubernatorial candidate Marsha Blackburn speaks at an election night event in Nashville. AP Photo/George Walker IV The Republican Tennessee senator became the first woman elected to serve as the state's governor. Blackburn defeated her Democratic opponent, Jerri Green, and will succeed GOP Gov. Bill Lee, whose term is limited after serving eight years in office. "We ran a different kind of campaign, focused on Tennesseans, not on the media's terms and not on any other candidate's terms," Blackburn told supporters in Nashville on election night. "We ran a campaign that was for the people of Tennessee, and we have proved that this is how you win. You build a campaign from the grassroots, from the bottom up, not the top down." Keisha Lance Bottoms Georgia Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms, right, embraces her daughter, on Tuesday in Atlanta. AP Photo/Brynn Anderson The former Atlanta mayor made history on two fronts in the 2026 midterms: she became the first Black woman governor in U.S. history, and the first woman governor of Georgia. The Democrat claimed victory over Republican billionaire Rick Jackson in the state's gubernatorial race. David Crowley Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley speaks on Tuesday night in Milwaukee. AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh The Democrat became Wisconsin's first Black governor after defeating his Republican opponent, Tom Tiffany. Crowley had dropped out of the gubernatorial race over the summer, but rejoined after Tony Evers, the outgoing Democratic governor, urged him to do so. Byron Donalds Florida Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds celebrates his election night win with his wife, Erika. via REUTERS / REUTERS The Republican congressman, endorsed by President Trump, will be Florida's first Black governor, succeeding Ron DeSantis, who reached his gubernatorial term limit. Aaron Ford Democratic gubernatorial candidate Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford speaks at an election night event in Las Vegas. AP Photo/John Locher Nevada's Democratic attorney general won the state's gubernatorial race, defeating Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, becoming the state's first Black governor. Ford previously made history as Nevada's first Black Senate majority leader and attorney general. Before he was first elected to the state legislature in 2012, he was an attorney at a private law firm and was a public school math teacher. Deb Haaland New Mexico Democratic gubernatorial candidate Deb Haaland waves to supporters on Tuesday in Albuquerque. Sam Wasson via Getty Images Haaland made history as the first Native American woman governor in U.S. history when she won New Mexico's gubernatorial race. The Democrat is a member of Laguna Pueblo. Gina Hinojosa Democratic Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa speaks to supporters on Tuesday in Austin. AP Photo/Ashley Landis The Democratic state congresswoman became Texas's first Latina governor after defeating Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who was seeking his fourth term. Amy Klobuchar Minnesota gubernatorial candidate Sen. Amy Klobuchar reacts at an election night event in St. Paul. AP Photo/Abbie Parr The Democratic U.S. senator became Minnesota's first elected woman governor on Tuesday when she defeated Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth. Klobuchar has broken glass ceilings in the state before: in 1998, she became the first woman elected Hennepin County attorney, and, in 2006, she became the state's first woman U.S. senator. articles.title: Mike Johnson won't seek reelection as House Republican leader
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — House Speaker Mike Johnson told staff on Wednesday morning that he would not run for minority leader after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections , two sources familiar with the announcement said. Johnson handily won reelection to his Louisiana congressional district. But members of his party lost across the country on an election night that will put Democrats in the majority in the House and Senate in the next legislative session. Among the likely contenders to try to replace Johnson as House leader are fellow Louisiana Rep. Steve Scalise, the current majority leader, and Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan, the current House Judiciary Committee chairman. Live updates: VP Vance blames Iran war for Dem landslide in House, Senate A person familiar with situation said Johnson did not want to get in the way of Scalise's ambitions. Scalise previously ran for speaker in 2023 but dropped out after he was unable to consolidate Republican support. Johnson went on to become speaker of the House. Some previous speakers have resigned their seats after stepping down, but Johnson is not expected to resign from Congress, a second person familiar with his thinking said. Johnson joked before the midterm election that he could return to his hometown of Shreveport and start a lawn-mowing business if Republicans were defeated. He later said it was a "tongue in cheek" comment. USA TODAY Exclusive: Mike Johnson reflects on balance of powers in Trump era He previously told USA TODAY during a June 29 interview that he intended to keep "steady hands at the wheel" of GOP leadership after the midterm election. "I intend to win the election and maintain the speakership. We have a lot more to do, and the last two years of the Trump administration will be just as epic as the first two. I intend to keep steady hands at the wheel," he said at the time. articles.title: World leaders question if GOP midterm losses will weaken or embolden Trump
articles.summary: Capitals from Kyiv to Tehran were closely watching the U.S. midterm elections for clues about the direction of Washington’s foreign policy after two erratic years that have put many leaders in conflict with President Donald Trump. Those eager to see the president put on his back foot woke up Wednesday to find Republican losses even greater than they expected. But with Democrats set to control both houses of Congress, U.S. allies and foes alike are now wondering whether Trump - weakened and stymied at home - will act more aggressively or unpredictably on the world stage, where the executive has far more unilateral muscle, as he strives to secure a legacy in his remaining two years in office. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. A Democratic Congress could attempt to rein Trump in on several fronts, from imposing war powers restraints on Iran and further cutting back weapons sales and other aid to Israel, to constraining his tariff policies and resuming direct aid to Ukraine. Implications for war in the Middle East Tehran, which was hoping for a blow to Trump, now faces the question of whether the president - after such a resounding rebuke of his war policy at the ballot box - will still feel emboldened to resume strikes, as he has threatened in the run-up to the midterms. On Wednesday, Iranian officials portrayed the Republican defeat as a public verdict on an unpopular and costly war. “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message. If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the Iranian parliamentary speaker, said on X. Trump acknowledged Tuesday night that the war in Iran was partially to blame for wide-scale Republican losses in the midterm elections, but insisted the results were not a disavowal of his presidency. The midterm results sent ripples of concern through Israel, which had closely followed a U.S. election that was often dominated by bitter debates over the war, its effect on the U.S. economy, the role of pro-Israel campaign donors and allegations of antisemitism. Democratic candidates such as Abdul El-Sayed and James Talarico, who won their Senate races in Michigan and Texas, respectively, have pledged to withhold weapons sales to Israel. They have also slammed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for a devastating Gaza campaign that has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians. The victories of so many Democrats who were critical of Netanyahu and Israel could spark “a sense of urgency” among Israeli opposition leaders to drop their differences and form a government to oust the current prime minister, said Yaakov Katz, a fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute, a think tank in Jerusalem. Just last week, Israelis held their own elections and denied Netanyahu a straightforward return to power, but neither did they hand challenger Gadi Eisenkot an easy path to form a majority government. “This will have to have an impact on what’s happening with coalition building because you can’t ignore the huge shift in the U.S.,” Katz said. “It’s now in your face: The current government, if it continues, will only cause more problems and challenges for Israel. It’s just too toxic.” On Wednesday, several leaders from Eisenkot’s bloc pointed to the midterm results and blamed Netanyahu for cratering Israel’s image in the United States. The centrist Yair Lapid said that the midterm results showed the opposition bloc must not strike a deal to join a government that included Netanyahu - something that Netanyahu has been pushing. “The American election results in the morning have one unexpected outcome: they eliminate any possibility of a unity government led by Netanyahu,” Lapid said on X. “Israel cannot afford to let him remain prime minister. It endangers security, it endangers democracy, it will crush us in the world.” Yair Golan, a left-leaning opposition leader, said Netanyahu had become “toxic among both Democrats and Republicans.” Netanyahu remaining in power “could lead Israel down a path of international sanctions, international isolation, and a clash with the U.S., our friend and most important ally,” he warned. Europe considers a weakened Trump The war in Ukraine has been one of the widest partisan divides in U.S. foreign policy, and it will soon be put to the test as U.S.-brokered talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations resume in Abu Dhabi next week, the first such meeting since February. In Moscow, officials have treated the results as a sign that Trump’s position on Ukraine may harden in Moscow’s favor, arguing that by betting on a Democratic victory, Kyiv and European capitals have aligned themselves with Trump’s chief political enemies at home and should now expect two years of a less constrained president in return. “They will not get a more pliable and constrained Trump,” Konstantin Kosachev, a Russian senator, said on Telegram. “They will get a more determined one, who no longer has to look over his shoulder at elections. For all the importance of Congress, the US president’s role in foreign policy takes priority, and Trump knows that better than everyone else put together.” The questions about Washington’s commitments to NATO and its other traditional allies, which emerged during Trump’s first presidency, led some Europeans back then to warn that U.S. interests inevitably would diverge from their own. Those differences have come into starker relief during Trump’s second term, as he pressed Europe to take responsibility for more of its own defense, turning his sights to Asia and the Middle East and away from Russia’s war in Ukraine. Now, European officials are urging their governments to stay the course as they seek to continue reducing their reliance on the U.S. as the continent’s key security guarantor. “Weakened Trump could become more aggressive and unpredictable. A lame duck could quickly turn into an angry duck,” Bernd Lange, a member of the European Parliament, said on X. “For EU, this is an opportunity and warning. More democratic influence could bring greater predictability and dialogue. But US protectionism won’t disappear. EU cannot live at Trump’s mercy!” The British government was careful to avoid showing any official pleasure with the Democratic takeover of Congress, knowing Trump is not yet halfway through his term. Privately, some officials expressed relief that that U.S. voters had delivered a check on a mercurial president who has upended transatlantic trade and security and produced a spike in fuel costs following his Iran war. And they expressed fear over how Trump - who seemed unleashed at the beginning of his second term - might act if he feels hemmed in by a hostile Congress. “You have to be aware that any president will still have enormous power to execute his foreign policy even if he finds himself more constrained by Democratic Congress at home,” said a British official who spoke on the condition of anonymity in order to share candid views. “Certainly, with this president, you have to be prepared for him to be even more volatile after this.” The view that Europe cannot afford to depend on Washington’s goodwill was echoed across Western Europe, where many called for continued support for Ukraine as a means of ensuring security on the continent. “Not because everything now changes for the better, but because it could benefit the support for Ukraine, the green transition, and relations with the rest of the world,” European Parliament vice president Christel Schaldemose said on X. “But the EU must ⁠continue the course of standing stronger and standing on its own two feet. That’s not up for debate.” The issue has gained urgency as Trump’s own backing for Kyiv has faltered, at times leading him to lash out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, whom he has blamed for the global energy disruptions even though the war in Iran has been the main contributor. Measured reactions in Asia The midterms are not expected to fundamentally change Washington’s approach to China, given the bipartisan consensus on strategic competition with Beijing, and across the region the prevailing expectation is that U.S. protectionist policies will continue regardless of who controls Congress. In Beijing, officials stuck to China’s traditional neutrality, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning calling the elections a domestic U.S. affair. She said Beijing was willing to work with Washington to “strengthen communication and manage differences.” Some analysts suggested that while the election would do little to the overall approach to China, it could still change how that competition plays out. “A Democratic-led Congress will certainly further intensify pressure on China on Taiwan, AI and export controls,” Zhao Minghao, a professor at Fudan University’s Institute of International Studies, told the South China Morning Post, adding that Democrats would likely scrutinize Trump’s engagement with Beijing more closely and could use China policy to challenge him politically. “This is a very big challenge for Beijing,” Zhao said, warning that Trump’s diminishing political authority could undermine recent progress toward a more stable relationship. Steve Hendrix, Natalia Abbakumova, Suzan Haidamous, Mohamad El Chamaa, Rudy Lu and Greg Miller contributed to this report. articles.title: Hegseth faces impeachment vote as Democrats prepare to take power
articles.summary: WASHINGTON – Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth faces impeachment accusations when Congress returns after the midterm elections and others, including President Donald Trump , could be investigated for alleged misconduct as Democrats return to power. Besides Trump and Hegseth, lawmakers have already filed impeachment resolutions against Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Education Secretary Linda McMahon . None of the resolutions gained traction while Republicans led the House, but they signal what Democrats could investigate when they take control of the House and Senate in January. The House impeached Trump twice while led by Democrats during his first term, over his dealings with Ukraine and over the Capitol attack on Jan. 6, 2021 . The Senate acquitted him both times for lack of a 2/3 majority to convict. But Democrats have filed at least four more impeachment resolutions against him for potential investigation. Impeachments have become more common but convictions remain elusive Any House member can introduce a resolution proposing to impeach the president, vice president, other executive officials or judges with accusations of "treason, bribery or other high crimes and misdemeanors." The process has led to the removal of eight federal judges but not anyone from the executive branch. Three presidents − including Bill Clinton in 1998 and Andrew Johnson in 1868 − and War Secretary William Belknap in 1876 have been impeached but not convicted. House Speaker Mike Johnson , R-Louisiana, has predicted another impeachment push against Trump with Democrats holding the gavel. Trump has said he expects to be impeached again with Democrats in control of House . He invited another showdown in June 2025 with the taunt: "go ahead and try Impeaching me, again, MAKE MY DAY!" Hegseth accused of unauthorized war in Iran, Venezuela Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Kentucky, launched his eight impeachment accusations against Hegseth on Sept. 15. The difference from other resolutions filed against Trump and his Cabinet secretaries months ago is that Massie plans to force a House vote on the measure as early as next week, when lawmakers return from the midterm elections. The Republican majority could kill it by voting to table it. But Massie accused Hegseth of conducting the war against Iran without congressional authorization, seizing Venezuela’s President Nicolas Maduro without constitutional authority and killing suspected drug traffickers in the Caribbean without judicial authorization. "Secretary Hegseth's constitutional violations extend beyond the illegal war in Iran,” said Massie, who lost his Republican primary and has only the lame duck session of Congress to pursue the impeachment resolution. “He is abusing the power of his office to ignore congressional war powers resolutions, to kidnap foreign leaders and to intimidate critics of the Trump administration by retaliating against them for exercising free speech.” Trump has defended Hegseth. "I think it's terrible. All they do is they talk about impeaching everybody," Trump told reporters Oct. 28 . "He's doing a great job. He's a great warrior. I think he's the best at his job in many many years and a lot of people agree with that." More: Trump's stinging midterm rebuke casts a new political landscape Congress could potentially move quickly if there is support for Massie's resolution. The House impeached Trump a week after the Capitol riot Jan. 6, 2021, and a week before he left office. The Senate acquitted him at trial in mid-February 2021. Trump would have been barred from federal office if convicted. Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson said in response to Massie's resolution that Hegseth is a "transformative leader" who has returned standards to the military and made the country's arsenal stronger than ever. "The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first," she said in a statement to USA TODAY . Wilson had called an earlier Democratic impeachment resolution "another charade in an attempt to distract the American people from the major successes we have had here at the Department of War." Trump, who endorsed Massie’s Republican primary opponent, has called him a “loser,” a "lightweight" and "a major sleazebag" for opposing the Iran war and voting against other administration priorities. Raskin outlines potential investigations of Trump Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, who led the second impeachment against Trump, argued that Trump has "undoubtedly" committed impeachable offenses. He cited the unauthorized war against Iran, spending money Congress hasn't authorized and bulldozing the East Wing of the White House. "They have been plundering money from our government in the most massively corrupt presidential administration in American history," Raskin told NBC's "Meet the Press." Raskin called impeachment "a critical tool in the toolbox" but that Congress could respond to Trump legislatively, too. "Impeachment is not a taboo with us, it's not a fetish with us, we understand it is not a panacea," Raskin said. "We will not hesitate to use it if we need to use it." Departing Democrats accuse Trump of unauthorized war, abuse of power and profiting from office Democrats have filed at least four impeachment resolutions against Trump during his second term. All four lawmakers have lost their seats, so the resolutions signal subjects for investigation next year. Rep. Shri Thanedar of Michigan, who lost his Democratic primary after four years in office, filed impeachment accusations against Trump in April 2025 . His accusations included alleged obstruction of justice from Trump firing Justice Department staffers who investigated Jan. 6 and for dropping charges against New York Mayor Eric Adams. Rep. John Larson of Connecticut, who lost his Democratic primary after 28 years in office, filed impeachment accusations against Trump in April for alleged belligerence without congressional authorization against Iran, Yemen, Lebanon, Syria, Nigeria and Gaza, and for threatening military force against Panama, Colombia, Cuba and Greenland. Larson also accused Trump of abuse of power in the immigration crackdown and of twisting law enforcement to investigate perceived political rivals. Rep. Al Green of Texas, who lost his Democratic primary after 22 years in office after Republicans redrew congressional maps in his state, has filed several impeachment resolutions against Trump , the latest in August over the seizure of Maduro . Rep. Steve Cohen, D-Tennessee, filed 26 impeachment accusations against Trump on Sept. 24 . Beyond the military allegations, Cohen accused Trump of abuse of power for his immigration crackdown, for his investigation of perceived rivals such as former FBI Director James Comey and for profiting from his office. “Trump is clearly the most impeachable President our country has ever endured," said Cohen, another longtime Trump antagonist who retired from his 20-year seat after GOP redistricting. "His continued presence in office is a danger to our democracy." Education Secretary McMahon accused of dismantling department but she aims to improve student performance Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, D-Oregon, filed impeachment allegations against Education Secretary Linda McMahon in June. The accusations covered significant staff reductions at the department and moving 140 programs and offices to other federal departments. “I introduced an impeachment resolution because Secretary McMahon has made it her mission to close down the Department of Education, something she does not have the right to do,” Bonamici said on the House floor. Trump has said he appointed McMahon to dismantle the department . McMahon responded to the impeachment allegations by arguing that Democrats were fine with historically low test scores, classrooms shuttered during the COVID-19 pandemic and allowing transgender athletes in female locker rooms. “It speaks volumes that House Democrats think an impeachable offense is working to improve student outcomes and reduce the federal bureaucracy,” McMahon said on social media in June . “To the Democrats in Congress: do better.” Health Secretary Kennedy accused of 'spreading conspiracy theories' but spokesperson calls allegations 'partisan theatrics' Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Michigan, filed impeachment accusations against Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in December. Stevens accused Kennedy of freezing or canceling billions of dollars in research, firing health advisers and spreading conspiracy theories. " Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has imperiled the health and safety of the American people, eroded public confidence in the nation’s public health institutions and stalled decades of scientific and medical progress ," Stevens wrote in the resolution. Andrew Nixon, the top department spokesperson, accused Stevens, who lost a Democratic primary for Senate this year and later endorsed the Republican opponent in the race , of playing political games. "Secretary Kennedy remains focused on improving Americans’ health and lowering costs, not on partisan theatrics designed to elevate standing in a failing, third-rate Senate bid," Nixon said in a statement to USA TODAY . articles.title: Democrats take control of Congress and put Trump's economic agenda in their sights
articles.summary: Democrats retook power in Washington on Tuesday, flipping key House and Senate seats to command majorities in both chambers of Congress. The power shift creates a new platform for Democrats to launch investigations of President Trump's economic allies — Elon Musk, to name one — and pass bills that may be unlikely to become law but will mark a sharp change in the political climate for business leaders and economic issues after two years of unified Republican control. The change also appears set to elevate figures like Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren and others to prominent positions with oversight over economic policy. Read more: What a Democratic sweep means for stocks Voter casts their ballot at a polling place on November 3 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Jim Vondruska/Getty Images) Jim Vondruska via Getty Images Democrats are planning "a shock-and-awe legislative sprint," the New York Times reported , on issues like healthcare subsidies and Trump's tariffs, which could prompt a wave of bills to pass the House but stall against the 60-vote threshold in the Senate. Even in the minority, Senate rules mean Republicans retain the power to stop legislation. Democrats are also likely to seek areas of bipartisan agreement on pharmaceuticals, the housing market, and AI data centers, all sectors that both Republicans and Democrats have spotlighted on the campaign trail. Divided government, of course, may also set the stage for political clashes that could destabilize markets and the broader economy. "While conventional wisdom suggests equities tend to rally following midterm elections, particularly when the outcome produces divided government, we caution that the post-election environment may look considerably different this cycle," Raymond James Washington Policy Analyst Ed Mills warned in a pre-election note. He added that much of the recent volatility has been driven by unexpected moves from the White House. "We believe Trump will increasingly test the limits of executive authority during the remainder of his term," Mills wrote. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York talks with phone bank volunteers during a midterm election night watch party in Washington on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images) Tom Williams via Getty Images 'Lawyer up': An expected focus on Elon Musk and Trump's economic team The House is set to be led by Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who has been notably tight-lipped about his plans . He met with Democratic volunteers as Election Day wound down and told reporters , "We're relentlessly focused on driving down the high cost of living and fighting for an affordable America." Jeffries avoided the question of whether he would reach out to Trump, while the president told the New York Times he will accept the election results . Going by early signals, Democrats intend to aim their new powers at an array of high-profile targets, with Musk chief among them, as part of a far-reaching effort to impose new checks on the Trump administration. "Lawyer up," said Rep. Robert Garcia, who is poised to become chair of the House Oversight Committee, in one particularly pithy signal of the Democrats' plans. Recent developments involving Elon Musk and Starlink in Ukraine are just the latest topic that Democrats say they will investigate around the world's richest man. The Wall Street Journal has reported that Musk ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink relied on by Ukraine and discussed the decision on a call with Trump in October. A group of Silicon Valley lawmakers said in a letter the issue raises broader concerns and could lead them to "closely scrutinize federal funding awarded to Mr. Musk's businesses" in the next Congress. Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk receives the National Medal of Science from President Donald Trump during Summit in Washington, DC in October. (Win McNamee/Getty Images) Win McNamee via Getty Images Musk could also face questions about his role in the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and SpaceX's other government contracts. Trump this week said he would consider preemptively pardoning officials like Musk who face legal scrutiny from Democrats, saying in an interview , "I would if I needed to, sure. I wouldn't even think about it." Capitol Hill observers are also expecting economic-themed clashes, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent potentially facing new scrutiny. Politico recently reported that Democrats are planning to investigate the Treasury Department and the IRS, as well as Trump's actions to rein in the power of financial regulatory agencies. Bessent's clashes with Democratic lawmakers have already been caustic and highly personal over the last two years, and that could only intensify as Democrats gain the power to subpoena documents and compel testimony, with Sen. Warren likely to lead the Senate's influential Banking Committee. This new subpoena power could also put an array of executives in the hot seat, from tech executives facing potential hearings over harmful AI-agent behavior to CEOs being called to answer allegations of price gouging across sectors. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent testifies during a House Financial Services Committee hearing in September. (ROBERTO SCHMIDT / AFP via Getty Images) ROBERTO SCHMIDT via Getty Images Sectors where 'investors might see a glimmer of hope' The changeover in power has implications — good and bad — for numerous business sectors. Democrats could seek to boost sectors like clean energy by blocking further efforts by Trump to cut tax credits. Stifel Chief Washington Policy Strategist Brian Gardner offered clean energy as the top potential winner in his final midterm election preview. "Investors might see a glimmer of hope that clean energy tax credits could be revived or extended," he wrote this week, adding that the credits "also have some GOP support so they could be revived even in a split Congress." Rep. Brendan Boyle, who is set to be the next chairman of the House Budget Committee, said in a statement, "I will fight to reverse his costly tariffs and devastating healthcare cuts, and bring an end to the war in Iran." Moves to reverse Trump's tariffs are almost sure to be met with a presidential veto, but more bipartisan areas could sidestep the president. Screengrab of a campaign ad from Mike Rogers. The housing issue earlier this year delivered a potential proof of concept when a major piece of legislation passed with bipartisan majorities and became law despite Trump's refusal to sign it . During the now-concluded campaign season, candidates from both parties focused criticisms on pharmaceuticals and AI data centers, a sign that these sectors may be ripe for bipartisan compromise. This story has been updated. Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance. articles.title: GOP officials describe 'reckoning' to come after party's midterm losses
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s allies on Wednesday tiptoed their way toward once unthinkable territory: blaming the president. The unusual candor followed sweeping GOP defeats across the country, a repudiation of the president that matched some of the party’s worst fears. Some pointed to the Iran war and its effect on gas and grocery prices. Others pointed to the president’s demeanor. “There's a little bit of a reckoning in the Republican Party about where they go,” said Matt Dole, chair of the GOP in deep red Licking County, Ohio. “I think you're going to see a part of the Republican Party advocate for a return to normalcy, which is not repudiating Trump's ideology and policies, but will repudiate Trump's style.” “It sounds a little ironic,” failed Maine Republican governor candidate Bobby Charles told POLITICO. “But I am nevertheless optimistic for the future because Trump's going to be gone in two years.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Trump and his advisers, meanwhile, blamed myriad factors, including Fox News, RINOs and “lazy” candidates — even as the party resoundingly lost both chambers of government and the blue wave rolled through deep red Texas, South Carolina, Iowa and Kansas. Trump singled out Texas GOP Gov. Greg Abbott, who he called a “RINO,” and absolved himself of blame, claiming Republicans would have won “in a landslide” had he been on the ballot. Abbott did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Trump adviser Alex Bruesewitz blamed the GOP’s poor performance on candidates he described as “uninspiring, lazy and thoroughly ineffective communicators” — explicitly calling out Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), who struggled throughout the course of his campaign to gain traction against Democratic incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff. The Collins campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment. One GOP operative working on multiple midterm races said it was a "lazy excuse" to blame candidate quality. "This is more than just one lazy candidate here. I mean, the chair of the … NRCC is losing his election.” Still, other Republicans turned their ire on the GOP-controlled Congress. “The Republican Party needs to have a conversation with itself about how to listen to the voters and present meaningful policy reform that impacts their lives,” said Gina Swoboda, the former chair of Arizona’s Republican Party and a longtime Trump ally. “This Congress did not do a single thing that I can name that meaningfully impacted the working class and middle class.” Bruesewitz expressed dismay that some of those candidates boarded Air Force One and left their states five days before Election Day, after Trump had traveled to campaign for them. “They’re so dependent and so reliant on the president,” Bruesewitz said. “The president’s strength has allowed Republicans to coast for a decade. His endorsement has cleared the field for them in their primaries and oftentimes in general elections. Most of them have never had to fight in a tough race, so they forgot the basics of campaigning and communicating in a digital era.” Top Trump officials had already hinted at that plan in interviews with POLITICO in the lead up to the election. Republicans on Capitol Hill and beyond, who have been preparing for the bloodbath and recriminations, were not buying it. They argued that flat characterization of Republican candidates as lazy could not possibly be applied to every vulnerable Republican who lost — and that Trump and the aides around him ought to look in the mirror. But tellingly, they refused to put their name behind it. "We are beyond candidate quality. It's a bloodbath," one senior Senate GOP official said. “Trump did this.” A Republican operative working on swing state campaigns said Tuesday was a perfect storm “of just incompetence.” “The people in the White House didn't do anything to stop him from engaging on things that were actively making everything worse because he was ignoring what the voters were caring about,” the operative said. articles.title: 美国中期选举如何重塑商品市场？
articles.summary: 今天只有一些碎片化的时间，所以我们也不啰嗦，就一个一个话题讨论过来 政治：我不觉得这是一次性的事情，这是未来两年美国政治风向的改变。 之前说过，中期选举是一个检验器，大家会根据这个投票，去看待说过去两年美国的很多政策能不能继续实施下去，虽然中期选举执政党一般都会有点问题，但这一次的情况显然是民主党的大胜。 2024年无论是投给Trump还是Harris的地区，在这一次投票中，给民主党的投票都增加了8%。 这是非常明显的民意转变，平心而论，除了物价之外，过去两年美国的经济其实没太多问题，当然话也可以反过来说，美国过去两年经济不错，但物价控制不好。 按照共和党自己的看法，输掉选举的主要原因，就是伊朗问题， 在12个月之前，大家没有人觉得民主党可以横扫共和党，而伊朗问题改变了一切。 包括大家看到的， 在一些数据中心建设多的地方，大家就投票民主党 ，这真的是一个非常简单的问题，只要你家边上有一个数据中心，你家的网速并不会变的更快，但电费就要增加一百到几百美元一年，然后如果是电取暖，你的房价可能就会下跌1-2%，所以大家是不是喜欢数据中心带来的就业，是的，但就是不喜欢这个东西在自己家边上。 物价问题，或者说可负担性问题，我觉得是共和党输掉选举的原因，这个和2024年是一样的。从这个角度说，2025年的关税日，2025年秋天的降息，以及2026年3月的伊朗问题，是大家不满积累的三个层面。 作为一个商品交易者，我的直观感觉是，这是一个警惕信号，我觉得联储也好，白宫也好，美国地方政府也好，在未来两年会更加慎重， 在很多刺激政策上会多一分小心，在破坏供应链上会多一分小心。在商品的整体思路上，我会从过去几年的货币+财政双宽松，供应链断裂的双重利好，变成看到降息和扩表才说需求逻辑，对于供应链断裂抱有更多警惕。 我觉得会有一天，商品价格回落，然后大家重新回到增长叙事，但站在目前，我的感觉是，美国人在经历了几年的高增长之后，不再珍惜这种高增长，而是想要控制通胀。 这就是联储那个dual mandate的灵魂拷问，不同时刻，到底是通胀更重要，还是失业率更重要。目前美国失业率没啥问题，美国民众这么不满肯定是对通胀不满。所以在未来两年，在做多商品的时候，我会更加小心一点。我不怀疑未来24个月联储有很大的概率会重新回到降息周期，我觉得商品的很多结构性做多因素都还在，但我觉得当美国人不满通胀的时候，我对于做多商品指数就是多一分谨慎。 地缘：平息，或者升级后再平息 短期我觉得结果无非这两种，美国人不想打仗，伊朗的最高领袖也说可以谈，双方可能谈不拢再打一架升级一下，就像上甘岭和第五次战役，但我觉得美国和伊朗都不太想打下去了。 油价的扰动可能是结构性的和长期的，但我觉得也许在2个月后，我们会看到这个战争走向自己最后的阶段。 这并不意味着长期问题的解决，我觉得中东已经被彻底改变，但我在想，比方说明天美国的航母开始轰炸伊朗，油价激增，这个时候，是看好说这个战争长期化的人多，还是觉得这个战争是最后的余波的人多，大家到底是追涨，还是sell the rally。我觉得这个问题是一目了然的。 利率：我觉得长端美债收益率可能短期见顶了，但这可能是熊市中的反弹 美国长端利率上行的核心，我觉得还是赤字率，以及太高的利息支出，在目前的利率中，实际利率我觉得很有可能短期见顶，因为大家不觉得AI可以带来更好的增长，至少短期不这样觉得，通胀预期如上所述，我觉得继续冲高的概率不大，民主党大胜，对于美元和美债的不确定性担忧也在减少，我不是利率的专家，但我觉得4.5%甚至以下的十年期美债收益率是完全有可能的。 但这并不能完全解决美债的问题，我觉得4.0-4.5%，或者宽容一点，3.5%-4.0%可能是十年期美债在未来很长时间的底部区间。 黄金：我觉得距离降息依然有距离，黄金的反弹是可能的，但还没有到它的主升浪 AI的退潮可能降低了实际利率的上行空间，美国的反战情绪让伊朗的扰动可能降低，联储进入加息周期的概率被降低了。 但如上所述，我觉得当美国人不满通胀的时候，通胀指标也没达标，联储几乎没有可能很快降息，除非发生经济风险。 所以我觉得黄金在这里反弹是有逻辑的，从最高点回撤35%差不多也就是3600左右，3700-3800也是很多技术点位的位置，打个底仓我觉得完全没毛病，之前我想在更低的位置去sell put，更靠近3700-3800。但市场没有走到也没办法。 这是不是个可以重仓的时候？我觉得依然有怀疑，我觉得目前的政治环境不支持大规模的货币+财政宽松，美国的是如此，中国也需要时间，所以这可能是一个反弹+震荡的过程，如果未来一切顺利，就是时间换空间，降息前底部提高，降息后上涨，如果未来出点问题，就是跌一把再买。 2018中期选举之后有美国高收益债的问题，2022年之后有SVB的暴雷，加息周期的过程中一帆风顺的概率不是那么高，所以我觉得不是重仓的时候。 铜 除了之前说的宏观与微观的矛盾之外，我觉得铜其实也可以说是一个美股问题，今天因为对于监管的担忧，市场基本上觉得很多数据中心的建设会有问题，一些neocloud和硬件厂商也遭遇了风险，但只要科技大厂依然愿意投资（他们的成本其实还降低了），那么对于AI，对于铜的叙事就还是Okay的。 我觉得铜的产业叙事，其实核心在于，当上游价格跌了一点之后，或者说科技大厂有机会吃掉一些过于激进的Neocloud之后，他们会不会继续稳定投资AI，对这个问题我其实并不知道。这个可能需要AI真的出来一些不错的应用。 另外就还是之前说的，如果宏观把铜干下去，下游库存并不高，结局可能类似2025年4月，无非斜率可能有些不同。如果下游补库存完成，比方说明年3月4月库存回到10-20万吨，然后宏观还是今天这个样子，那可能类似2023年夏天，大家发现预期没那么好，距离降息还有段距离。 坦率说放在未来2年时间维度，我觉得铜的长期叙事有两个事情是萦绕在我心头的。 1，我知道未来的供给预期不一定非常顺利，很多扰动都会发生。尤其是美国如果战略收缩，资源民族主义只会更多而不是更少。 2，我觉得过去两年的叙事非常有利于铜，而美国人已经对这个叙事投了反对票。 把这些合在一起，就是我此时对铜的看法，有大跌我愿意买，没有跌我觉得兴趣不大，因为我觉得它的空间也不会太大。 最后我想作为收尾的话，在2025年年底，我曾经画了一个四象限，说2026年最有可能的两个情况是： 2025年的延续，AI不错，其他大家都糟糕 2025年的翻转，AI有点问题，利率走低，其他行业好起来 当时我觉得后者概率大一点，结果上下半年各交易了一次逻辑 今天对于商品，我在想2027年的思路时候，我的第一反应是，当美国，甚至很多地方的国家都在努力遏制通胀时，全面做多大宗商品，要么需要通胀被控制住（也许又有那种空油多一切其他商品的思路），要么需要一个危机，这个危机如果发生在新兴市场，更类似1997年，如果发生在美国，更类似2018年。 我觉得过去几个月，因为中期选举和9月FOMC的加息，很多大宗商品价格都出现了明显的回落，我们可能都希望能快速回到那个做多的世界里，但从政治的角度，这次中期选举反对的，就是过去几年那种降息后的物价上涨，我觉得反弹是完全可能的，但对我来说，在通胀被控制到联储开心之前，我觉得全面做多的需求逻辑都是存疑的。 这是非常第一时间的想法，我有很长的时间可以在旅途中再想想，到了周末我觉得会有更全面的思路。 articles.summary: 11月3日晚间，监管机构官网披露了《关于核准泉果基金管理有限公司变更持股5%以上股东的批复》。 相关批复显示，监管核准了泉果基金创始人、总经理李云亮，上海泉至清企业管理中心（有限合伙）（以下简称泉至清)，上海泉至澈企业管理中心（有限合伙）（以下简称泉至澈）成为泉果基金持股5%以上股东。对李云亮、泉至清、泉至澈分别受让泉果基金600万元、427.01万元、624.99万元人民币出资（分别占注册资本比例6%、4.2701%、6.2499%)无异议。 据接近泉果的人士透露，上述股权来自于泉果基金创始人、原总经理王国斌。原由王国斌持有的35%股权，未来将变更至公司员工持有。相关安排体现了泉果团队和公司未来长期、深度绑定的坚定信心。 三主体增持泉果股权 泉果基金成立于2022年2月，注册资本1亿元。公开信息显示，泉果基金初始股权结构为：泉果基金董事长任莉、原总经理王国斌各持股35%，姜荷泽和李云亮分别持股7.04%和3%，4个员工持股平台各持股4.99%。 由于泉果基金一开始即采用“核心股东+员工持股平台”的架构，四家员工持股平台——泉至清、泉至澈、泉至澄、果至行在公司成立之初即已设立，旨在通过股权纽带，将股东、公司与核心员工的长期利益深度绑定，并构成面向长期可持续发展的制度性安排。 证监会上述批复显示，李云亮和泉至清、泉至澈两大员工持股平台分别受让6%、4.2701%、6.2499%的泉果基金股权。这意味着，此次股权变更完成后，李云亮和上述两大员工持股平台将持有泉果基金9%、9.2601%和11.2399%的股权。 泉果首次员工持股计划推进中 值得关注的是，泉果基金今年还将启动首次员工持股计划。从上述两大员工持股平台的股权变动来看，这一重要事项大概率已有了积极进展。 据知情人士透露，此次首批员工持股计划覆盖范围较为广泛，投研、市场、合规、风控、产品、运营、IT等前中后台岗位均有涉及。 “我们希望持续汇聚资产管理行业具有长期竞争力的优秀人才，通过员工持股平台等长效激励机制，提升核心团队的稳定性和自主创造性，让大家共同成长、共创价值。”泉果董事长任莉在公司成立之初就阐述过自己的人才观。 任莉认为，对泉果而言，个体的优秀很重要，但团队内部的专业互补、彼此协同、形成合力更重要。“多元、丰富、平衡的生态是最有生命力的。” 业内人士认为，泉果基金通过推行员工持股等机制安排保持核心团队稳定、促进公司长久健康发展，显然是一个具备长期战略思维的重要举措。股权激励的核心作用在于吸引并且留住优秀人才，泉果的做法显然有助于公司提升投研实力，强化内部治理，提升管理水平和整体竞争力。 投研骨干走上管理岗位 此时回看，泉果基金自年初以来，进行的一系列重要人事调整，显得筹谋长远、意味深长。 这些人事动作包括：李云亮由合规负责人、风控负责人转任总经理，全面负责泉果基金的日常经营管理； 副总经理姜荷泽兼任财务负责人。 知名基金经理、公募投资部总经理赵诣新任公司副总经理。 高管团队中，韦海菁、姚钟骁等升任副总经理；孙媛任合规负责人、风控负责人。 经过多年的持续打磨，如今的泉果基金人才梯队较为完备、核心投研人才稳定迭代，权益投资、固收投资、量化投资等都有布局，复合型专家型投研团队初步成型，这些投资人才各展所长、共同进化，既保证了公司投资能力和策略的多样性，也形成了公司长期运营和文化传承的“底座”。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 一线直击香港金融科技周：机器人谈复购，智能体找入口
articles.summary: 今年的香港金融科技周，AI无疑是核心议题。 11月2日，第11届香港金融科技周x StartmeupHK 2026在香港拉开帷幕，活动将持续至11月6日。在已经举行的两天主论坛上，除了银行、保险、支付等传统金融科技议题，具身智能、自动驾驶、算力基础设施乃至商业航天等前沿产业，成为讨论焦点。 这场举办了十余年的行业大会，正在突破传统金融科技的边界。 香港金融科技周承办方Finoverse联合创始人兼联席首席执行官Vila Wong向华尔街见闻表示，过去大会主要吸引银行、保险及大型金融科技企业参与，如今越来越多AI企业和科技初创公司加入。今年大会超过一半的讨论内容与AI相关，投资者通行证申领量也创下历年新高。 变化不仅发生在参会企业和论坛议题上。 在具身智能领域，企业开始讨论机器人量产、模型与硬件协同、商业化交付等问题；在传统金融行业，AI智能体则正在尝试进入银行尽调、保险理赔、财富管理，甚至支付和投资交易等具体业务流程。 从前沿科技的产业化探索，到金融机构的实际业务应用，AI正在成为贯穿本届香港金融科技周的一条主线。 边界越来越宽 香港金融科技周的参与者越来越多元。 按照大会此前公布的预计规模，本届活动将汇聚来自120多个经济体的逾4.5万名参与者、超过1000位演讲嘉宾，以及800余家赞助商、参展商和初创企业。 Vila Wong向华尔街见闻回忆，2024年前后，金融科技周开始进一步细分不同产业领域，将保险科技、绿色科技等议题纳入讨论范围。 2025年，香港金融科技周首次与StartmeupHK创业节联合举办，进一步吸引了科技初创企业参与。相比过去以成熟金融机构为主的参会结构，大会开始覆盖更广泛的科技产业。 今年，这一趋势继续延伸。本届主论坛共设置10个专题论坛，涵盖政策与前瞻、AI与前沿科技、金融AI、保险科技及健康科技、绿色科技、创业家及创投、科技建设者以及创作者等方向。 尽管金融依然是大会的重要组成部分，但越来越多议题已经延伸到金融之外。 具身智能正是今年受到关注的前沿产业之一。 在一场围绕机器人产业化瓶颈的圆桌讨论中，星尘智能联合创始人兼CFO方科、擎朗智能创始人兼CEO李通等企业代表参与讨论，重点关注机器人从零部件、模型到完整系统的产业化挑战。 这些讨论也折射出具身智能行业正在面临的新变化。随着通用大模型能力快速进步，具身智能企业需要重新思考自身的技术壁垒。 方科向华尔街见闻表示：“我们把 具身模型与通用大模型看作是伙伴关系，是要发挥各自强项，携手并进。我们不是投降派，也不是抵抗派，是第三派：保持开发，既要又要派。” 他举例称，机器人可以借助通用大模型理解复杂指令，但在真实物理环境中，感知物体重量、判断受力情况以及完成抓取等动作，仍然需要具身模型自身具备判断和执行能力。 因此，星尘智能目前仍坚持自研具身模型、具身操作系统AOS和绳驱机器人本体协同发展的技术路线，同时借助通用大模型提升机器人的任务理解能力。 技术之外，商业化也成为具身智能企业必须面对的问题。 方科观察到，过去投资者更关心机器人能否完成复杂动作、模型是否具备泛化能力；如今，投资者开始进一步关注订单交付、客户复购以及软件服务能否产生持续收入。 “订单要看能不能交付，收入要看能不能持续。”方科表示，盈利也并不意味着要求早期企业现在就赚钱，更重要的是能否在扩大交付规模的同时降低成本，以及客户是否愿意为软件和服务持续付费。 类似的讨论还延伸到了其他前沿科技领域。今年大会还设置了太空经济与家族办公室投资相关议题，讨论商业航天项目的投资逻辑、风险评估以及长期资本如何参与产业发展。 参会资本的关注点同样呈现出差异。 Vila Wong提到，近年来中东投资者参与香港金融科技周的热情有所提升。这类投资者相对更关注基础设施，以及具有海外扩张能力的中大型成熟企业，希望通过投资和合作推动项目在当地落地。 与此同时，近年来赴港参加金融科技周的内地企业和创业者也有所增加。围绕中国企业与全球市场的连接，大会进一步设置专门的交流论坛。 科技企业、金融机构和投资者在同一场大会上寻找的机会越来越多，而如何让技术从研发走向实际应用，也成为不同产业共同面对的问题。 金融智能体嵌入工作流 金融科技周的议题不断向前沿科技延伸，传统金融行业的AI应用也在发生变化。 过去，金融机构使用AI，主要集中在智能客服、信息检索、文本生成和辅助分析等环节。如今，随着AI智能体逐渐具备调用工具、访问业务系统和执行复杂任务的能力，越来越多科技企业开始尝试让AI参与银行信贷、保险理赔、投资研究乃至资金支付等实际业务。 这种变化也反映在今年的论坛设置中。 在金融AI论坛一场名为“The Great AI Convergence”的圆桌讨论中，汇丰银行、道富银行以及企业AI公司Wonderful的代表，围绕AI如何从单一试点走向银行规模化应用展开讨论，涉及传统业务系统对接、数据分散以及投资回报等实际问题。 从这些讨论来看，金融机构对AI的需求已经开始超越简单的信息问答，希望将其逐步纳入专业业务流程。 在金融智能体的实际应用方面，腾讯也展示了针对银行、保险及资管等行业的解决方案。 在金融科技周期间举办的金融行业AI解决方案分享会上，腾讯WorkBuddy金融版展示了面向银行、保险及资产管理等行业的业务工作台。 在银行对公授信场景中，WorkBuddy通过9个不同分工的专家智能体，协同完成企业资料核验、财务分析、风险识别及尽职调查报告撰写等工作；保险领域的应用涉及理赔邮件识别、客户材料提取和辅助审核；在资产管理领域，AI则可以协助完成市场复盘、行业研究和投资分析。 这些场景展示了AI协同执行专业任务的能力，不过部分功能仍处于模拟演示阶段，实际部署效果仍需验证。 在海外市场，金融机构对模型选择、系统连接和数据安全的要求，也成为企业AI产品需要适配的环节。 腾讯WorkBuddy国际版相关人士向华尔街见闻表示，相较于国内版本，国际版支持GPT、Gemini等海外模型，也允许企业接入自行部署的模型；金融版则预置股票分析、投研报告、银行营销等专业技能，并进一步强化数据访问和权限管理。 目前，WorkBuddy国际版可在欧洲、中东和东南亚使用，销售采取直销和合作伙伴分销两种模式。其中，本地合作伙伴也可以面向所在市场的企业和行业客户销售产品。 支付方面，蚂蚁数科在金融科技周展示了“AI智能体超级工厂”解决方案，核心平台为Agentar，支持智能体开发、部署及规模化管理。同时，蚂蚁数科升级旗下ZOLOZ安全品牌，推出面向AI智能体的KYA身份治理方案，探索智能体身份验证、授权及安全管理等问题。 这些方案试图解决同一个现实问题：当AI开始代表企业或用户执行金融任务，如何确保其行为始终处于可授权、可控制、可追溯的范围内。 随着应用场景不断深入，技术能力只是其中一道门槛。企业还需要证明AI能够在真实业务中稳定运行，满足行业的安全要求，并创造可持续的商业价值。 当AI从回答问题走向执行任务，能否真正获得企业和用户的信任，将成为其进入金融核心业务的关键。 风险提示及免责条款 articles.title: 华为智驾之外，车企给出“Plan B”
articles.summary: 作者 | 周智宇 前几年，哪款车能率先用上新一代华为乾崑智驾，是新车发布会上的一个看点。如今，拿着相近的预算挑一辆家用SUV或MPV，买家已经能找到不止一款搭载同档乾崑的车。 市场的变化，已反映在车企的价目表上。11月3日，东风奕派M8加推两款天元激光版。三个多月前，这款六座SUV上市，五个版本用的都是华为乾崑。用车企习惯的话术，是“标配华为乾崑”。 不过这次，东风保留了原来的乾崑版，又给纯电车型配上了自家的辅助驾驶和座舱，把纯电M8的起步指导价从19.98万元降到17.98万元。 乾崑依然是块好招牌。尤其对从燃油车转过来的品牌，消费者原本熟悉的是它的发动机、底盘和空间，有了华为，少费些口舌就能让人愿意试一试它的智驾。只是当同级车也用上了同一套系统，这份好感会把人带进哪家店，就难说了。 眼下，一款车型的热销期已大幅缩短，靠首搭一套智驾方案赢来的优势，却可能只有几个月。过去大家抢的是谁先用上华为乾崑智驾，如今几家店都有华为乾崑智驾，车企更费心思的，是让顾客有个非来自己店里不可的理由。 当隔壁那辆车也有乾崑 11月3日，东风奕派M8天元激光版上市。谈起这两款车，奕派科技销售公司总经理邓留超专门说到了电芯，各个版本“不搞高低配区别”。17.98万元的纯电入门款，依旧用宁德时代的电芯、800V平台，标称续航600公里。 跟7月上市的纯电入门款相比，奕派M8天元激光版起价低了两万元。东风保留了原有的乾崑版，又给纯电M8增加了天元智驾的选择。这套系统基于地平线征程6M计算平台，搭配禾赛激光雷达。 而在三个月前，东风主打的是奕派M8标配华为乾崑。 据奕派9月初披露，首批车主中有80.6%在提车当天就开通了华为ADS高阶包。只是东风当初指望这辆车卖得更多。5月，M8在武汉首秀，时任东风奕派营销事业部总经理余岳峰说，“我们瞄准月销过万”。按太平洋汽车的车型销量数据，M8在8月和9月的销量都没到2000辆。 十几万元买辆带乾崑的六座SUV，已经有车做出了规模。譬如上汽通用五菱的华境S，15.98万元的入门款就有华为智驾。 据华境汽车披露，6月华境S交付5689辆，7月越过7000辆，此后几个月还在小幅往上走，10月交付了7507辆。9月13日起，华境S陆续从上市时的ADS Pro增强版升级到ADS 5 Pro。 在东风推天元版之前，手握近二十万元预算的买家，在这两辆六座车上已经能用到同一档乾崑。 不过一位最后选择了奕派M8乾崑版的车主告诉华尔街见闻，他在选择车型时，也有过纠结。华境S空间更大，价格合他的心意，也有他想要的华为智驾。最后提回家的是奕派M8乾崑版。他一直想买辆纯电车，华境S没有。 东风这次加推的两款天元版，恰好都放在了纯电M8上。 在四五十万元的MPV市场，岚图对哪些人也在看别家的车，有过一个估算。岚图汽车首席品牌官、销售公司总经理邵明峰在谈及岚图梦想家9用户群时，他点了智界V9的名，“我们和智界V9的用户重叠度超过70%”。按他的观察，这些人普遍看重华为的辅助驾驶。梦想家9全系标配华为乾崑ADS 5。 讲到自家车的长处，邵明峰把辅助驾驶的功劳给了华为，说到底盘驾控，他提的是岚图自己的虎踞底盘P。这辆MPV上，三腔空气悬架和双阀减振器都是岚图为乘坐舒适性下的本钱。 传祺也遇到过这桩难题。2025年2月，搭载华为ADS 3.0和鸿蒙座舱的岚图梦想家插混版，起价降到了35.99万元。三个月后，传祺向往M8乾崑上市，同样是插混MPV，同样的华为智驾和座舱，连35.99万元的起价都一样。 有车企营销人士对华尔街见闻表示，他们当前在对车型做营销时，遇到的一个问题就是，乾崑版与竞品的智驾同源，价格又挨得近。观众记住乾崑，几款车都可能沾光。对于品牌来说，反而难打出个性化。 现在去传祺的门店，向往M8已经有了不同的卖法。北京一家广汽传祺经销商挂出的报价单上，用Momenta的向往M8 PHEV L从26.48万元起，四驱顶配报30.48万元。同一张单子上，两款乾崑版分别报34.49万元和38.49万元。 PHEV L顶配和乾崑入门款之间差了四万元，消费者可以根据自己喜好做出选择。 PHEV L上市后三个月，已是向往M8卖得最多的一款。按汽车之家终端销量的排量分组推算，6月至8月，PHEV L卖了约1309辆，占同期向往M8销量的73%。车系总量也曾跟着涨过一阵，从5月的423辆升到6月的650辆、7月的660辆，8月又回落到482辆。单看版本占比，很容易高估这次加推带来的增量。算上其他版本，8月比5月多卖了59辆。 把订单留在 自己 店里 新车刚上市，销售要让尽可能多的人记住它。“全系标配乾崑”四个字，从入门到顶配都讲得通。等到要把销量再往上做，车企面对的却是那些已经看过车、仍然没有下单的人。他们未必都嫌车贵，有的人只是觉得，同样一笔钱，还有别的花法。 邵明峰说起过一种容易被总销量盖住的差别。有的用户提车后很快学会了自动泊车，也有人上高速、进城区都愿意自己开，用得着辅助驾驶，是在停车或需要主动避让的时候。同样选了一辆带乾崑的MPV，最让车主觉得钱花得值的功能，也可能只是每天回家停进那个窄车位。 从公司用车做到家庭用车，车企最容易想到的是把价钱降下来。可一个手握二十七八万元的买家，去年就买得起传祺向往M8宗师版。入门指导价26.99万元，今年6月推出的PHEV L前驱入门款是26.98万元。只看这100元的价差，很难理解传祺为什么做这种更新。 传祺动的是入门款能买到的东西。此前宗师版的入门款，标称纯电续航136公里，要用Momenta的城区领航辅助，还得往上买一档。 新推的PHEV L把前驱入门款的标称纯电续航加到了248公里，城区领航辅助也一起配上。10月26日，传祺又开始分批给这款车推送软件更新。遇上太窄的车位，车主可以先下车，再让车泊进去。对于平时自己开一辆大MPV上下班的人，充一次电能多开几天，在自家车库能不能从容下车，都是在二十七八万元那一档能比较的东西。 不过，家里要添一辆MPV，备选也不只新能源车。按太平洋汽车的车型销量榜，今年9月，丰田赛那以5849辆重回MPV销量首位。岚图在3月卖30.99万元的梦想家冠军版时，邵明峰讲过厂家的考虑，过去是“司机开、老板坐”，如今更多家庭是“爸爸开、全家坐”。 赛那这样的合资油混MPV本来就能把后排照顾得很好，想让这样的家庭换车，也得让那个亲自开车的人觉得值得。冠军版于是把华为乾崑和前双叉臂、后五连杆全铝悬架一起带进了三十万元价位。 在岚图，愿意买自研方案的顾客本来就有不少。岚图汽车销售服务有限公司副总经理李博晓此前透露，选择梦想家全车系的用户里，华为智驾版和自研智驾版的销量大约一比一。 5月15日，岚图汽车科技股份有限公司董事长卢放在轩辕汽车蓝皮书论坛上谈起这款车是怎么开发的。买梦想家，一套是华为乾崑智驾配鸿蒙座舱，另一套是岚图的鲲鹏智驾配逍遥座舱。 按卢放的说法，两种配置在外观上略有区别，底下却是同一个平台。岚图在开发时统一了许多底层技术，上面既能装自家的智驾和座舱，也能装华为的。到了卖车的时候，两套方案各有多少人选，在他看来，也是公司内部的一场“比赛”。 卢放说的这场“比赛”，岚图倒不急着分出胜负。之前自研版在梦想家上卖了将近一半，到最近，岚图照样把梦想家9的三个版本都给了乾崑。 对那些既看梦想家9、也看智界V9的人，华为智驾本来就是他们挑车的条件。而在二十七万元上下做家用MPV的生意，传祺只把入门价调低了100元，却把纯电续航从136公里加到了248公里。同一笔预算，买家更舍不得哪样东西，车企各有各的判断。 过去，一句“标配华为”就能让人愿意来试车。如今这句话依然管用，只是车企还得拿出竞争者没有的东西。顾客看中了车，却觉得眼前这款贵了些，或者更想把钱花在续航上，车企就有理由在乾崑版之外再做一个版本。这个“Plan B”争的，就是那些已经进了自家门、却可能去别家下单的人。 风险提示及免责条款 articles.title: 跌破50美元/盎司！白银：流动性冲击下的高贝塔清算
articles.summary: 10月30日，全球贵金属市场继续遭遇集中抛售：现货白银跌破50美元/盎司，日内跌幅超6%，为2025年11月以来首次跌破50美元/盎司关口；10月累计下跌约18%，较1月高点121.67美元/盎司回撤约60%。现货黄金跌至3880美元/盎司附近，月跌约6.6%，较年初高点回撤约30%。从盘面上看，白银在本次下跌中所展现出的弹性与破坏力显著强于黄金，反映出其高贝塔属性在市场流动性收紧时被进一步放大。 本轮贵金属下跌与2月底美伊冲突初期高度相似：主权国家和资本市场同时通过出售黄金换取美元流动性。前者用于补充能源进口、汇率干预和外部融资所需的美元；后者用于追加保证金、降低杠杆和应对赎回。 特别是近期AI资产遭遇持续抛售，科技巨头财报季成为风险偏好回落的催化剂：谷歌、英特尔、亚马逊等财报或资本开支指引不及预期，纳斯达克指数单日下跌近3%，科技股去杠杆压力向贵金属传导。黄金因流动性好而成为优先变现资产，白银则因替代属性和更高贝塔，在下跌过程中波动更大。 尽管此前 部分央行作为黄金市场的幽灵卖家抛售黄金、带动金价回落 ，黄金ETF等资金流向一度保持平稳，但近期AI财报引发权益市场剧烈波动，已使这部分资金开始加速撤离贵金属。 白银跌破50美元，反映的仍是流动性冲击
